stages.name: Reducing poverty and inequality
stages.title: Reducing poverty and inequality
stages.sub: How governments try to close the gap between rich and poor, and why those measures are hard to judge.

steps.q: A pensioner with no income is given £150 a week by the government, funded from taxes on everyone else. What happens to her income?
steps.hint: Money has moved from taxpayers straight into her pocket. Does her income change?
steps.pre: Direct cash transfers to those on low incomes are called

steps.q: Ali earns £20,000 and pays 20% tax. Bo earns £100,000 and pays 40% tax. As income rises, does the share paid in tax rise too?
steps.right: Yes, the rate rises with income
steps.wrong: No, the rate stays the same for everyone
steps.hint: Compare the two percentages, not the two pound amounts.
steps.pre: A tax whose rate rises as income rises is called

steps.q: A cleaner is legally paid £6 an hour. The government makes it illegal to pay below £11 an hour. What happens to her pay, by law?
steps.right: It must rise to at least £11
steps.hint: The law sets a floor. Can an employer legally pay below that floor?

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 3 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: Benefits, progressive tax and a wage floor are all things a government actively puts in place to shrink the income gap. What are they, together?
steps.right: Deliberate policy tools to cut inequality
steps.wrong: Side effects of running fiscal policy
steps.hint: Are these accidental results, or things chosen on purpose to close the gap?

steps.q: Raising the minimum wage helps low earners, but could it also make firms cut jobs or raise prices? Is judging these policies as simple as just listing their benefits?
steps.right: No, the downsides must be weighed too
steps.wrong: Yes, listing the benefits is enough
steps.hint: Think about the earlier point that higher taxes and benefits can change how hard people choose to work.
steps.pre: Weighing the benefits against the costs and side effects is the

steps.q: To set the right minimum wage or target the right households for benefits, the government needs to know exactly how firms and families will react. Does it ever have that perfect knowledge in advance?
steps.right: No, its data and forecasts are imperfect
steps.wrong: Yes, its data and forecasts are exact
steps.hint: Think about how deficit-reduction plans also rely on forecasts that can turn out wrong.
